extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, in-house counsel, and inventors in the biopharmaceutical/diagnostics space
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating and drafting biopharmaceutical diagnostic method claims under the Mayo v. Prometheus §101 framework, including how to identify laws of nature, whether claims add 'significantly more', and drafting strategies to avoid rejections. Focused on diagnostics (biomarkers, assays, metabolite correlations) and how to claim them post-Mayo.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 101 patent eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 101 defines patent-eligible subject matter: any new and useful process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter, subject to statutory exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statute is a broad 'coarse filter' for eligibility; courts recognize exceptions for laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas which are not patentable. Eligibility under §101 is distinct from novelty (§102), nonobviousness (§103), and §112 issues, but Mayo has blurred those lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions: laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: "[L]aws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas are not patentable."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims reciting purely natural relationships (e.g., correlations between biomarker levels and disease/treatment outcome) fall within these exceptions and are not patent eligible absent additional inventive contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1 — Is the inventive concept a law of nature?
rubrics_metrics.description: The initial §101 inquiry is whether the inventive concept of the method claim is a law of nature (a natural relationship).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the Court characterized claims in Mayo as describing relationships between metabolite concentrations and treatment efficacy — a natural relationship. If the inventive concept is a natural law, proceed to the 'significantly more' inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2 — Does the remainder of the claim add 'significantly more'?
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim's inventive concept is a natural law, determine whether the rest of the claim adds 'significantly more' than the natural law itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actions that are purely conventional, routine, or well-understood do not add 'significantly more' (per Mayo). The analysis purports to view the claim as a whole, but focuses on whether additional steps meaningfully transform or apply the natural law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conventional or obvious steps cannot rescue a natural law claim
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court found that purely conventional or obvious methods (e.g., well-known methods of determining metabolite levels) do not impart patent eligibility to a claim that centers on a natural law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novelty and nonobviousness concepts from §102/§103 were, for the first time, invoked in the §101 analysis; practitioners should not rely on routine assay steps to confer eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administering a known drug may be only an audience-identifying step
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'administering' step that involves giving a known drug for a known condition may be treated as merely identifying the intended audience (e.g., doctors) rather than transforming the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mayo treated the administering step as not adding 'significantly more' because it involved administering a known therapy; distinguish administering a new/man-made compound versus routine use of known drugs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transformations/manipulations as physical application (pre-Mayo view)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior to Mayo, steps showing transformation or manipulation of a sample or subject (e.g., administering a drug, manipulating blood in an assay) were viewed as active steps that could render a method patent eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-Mayo practice counted physical transformations and sample manipulations as evidence the claim was more than an abstract recitation of a correlation. Post-Mayo, such steps may be scrutinized for conventionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novel biological relationships alone risk being characterized as a natural law
rubrics_metrics.description: A newly discovered correlation or relationship between a biomarker and a disease/treatment outcome, without more, can be characterized as a law of nature and thus not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnostics often arise from insights about biological relationships; under Mayo, those insights alone are insufficient — the claim must include additional inventive subject matter beyond the mere recognition of the relationship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid making the 'law of nature' the central part of the claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not draft claims where the natural law (e.g., a correlation between a biomarker and outcome) is the central claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim centers on the natural relationship, it is vulnerable under Mayo. Structure claims to emphasize applied techniques, novel reagents, specific interventions, or inventive steps beyond mere recognition of the relationship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using solely general 'determining' steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Generic 'determining' or measurement steps presented without technical detail are likely to be considered purely conventional and will not make a claim patent eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims should avoid vague 'determine' language and instead recite specific, novel methods, apparatus, or data-processing steps that materially transform the sample or information in a nonconventional way.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize anything 'out of the ordinary' in the method
rubrics_metrics.description: Highlight and claim features that are not routine or conventional — anything that is out of the ordinary in the assay or method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novel sample-processing steps, specific reagents, nonconventional protocols, or inventive integration steps may help demonstrate that the claim adds 'significantly more' than a natural law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attempt to characterize the relationship as not being a natural law
rubrics_metrics.description: Draft claims and describe the invention in ways that argue the claimed relationship is not a mere natural law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This may involve emphasizing inventive laboratory techniques, engineered molecules, or other man-made aspects that transform or apply the relationship in a patent-eligible manner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine diagnostics with computing or other inventive technology
rubrics_metrics.description: Pairing traditional life-science diagnostics with computing functions (e.g., algorithms that determine correlations based on detected levels) or other technical elements may help avoid Mayo rejections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims to combined systems/methods that include technical, nonconventional computing steps or inventive data processing can provide the 'significantly more' needed for eligibility; be careful to claim specific technical implementations rather than abstract algorithms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require greater specificity in assay claims post-Mayo
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-Mayo, diagnostic method claims will require more specificity as to how the assay is performed and what technically differentiates it from routine practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General descriptions of assays are insufficient. Provide concrete parameters, steps, reagents, instruments, thresholds with technical justification, and any novel sample handling or measurement techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate existing patents and applications for Mayo vulnerability
rubrics_metrics.description: Existing applications and patents should be evaluated for vulnerability to Mayo-style §101 rejections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If not yet evaluated, practitioners should review and discuss options (e.g., claim amendments, divisional filings, emphasizing inventive aspects) for affected diagnostic claims.
